ALB requires subnets in at least 2 AZs

concepts.name: Multi-AZ versus multi-Region: choosing the blast radius
concepts.explain:
Multi-AZ protects against the loss of a data centre or an AZ inside one Region. It is cheap, mostly a configuration flag, keeps a single endpoint, and has sub-minute to low-minutes failover. It does not protect against a Regional service event, a Region-wide control plane problem, a bad deployment that you replicated everywhere, or a data-corruption bug — those need either multi-Region or point-in-time recovery.
Multi-Region costs materially more: duplicated infrastructure, cross-Region data transfer, replication lag (so a non-zero RPO unless you use a globally replicated data layer), more complex deployments, and DNS or Global Accelerator on top for traffic steering. The data layer decides what is feasible: Aurora Global Database gives typically sub-second cross-Region replication with roughly a one-minute RTO for a managed planned failover and cross-Region read scaling; DynamoDB global tables give multi-active writes with last-writer-wins conflict resolution; S3 Cross-Region Replication is asynchronous with S3 Replication Time Control offering a 15-minute SLA; RDS cross-Region read replicas and cross-Region automated backup replication are the cheaper, higher-RPO options.
For the exam, map the requirement to the smallest sufficient blast radius. 'Survive an AZ failure' → Multi-AZ. 'Survive a Region failure' → multi-Region plus a DR strategy chosen for the stated RTO/RPO. 'Survive accidental deletion or corruption' → versioning, PITR, backups, and Vault Lock — not more replicas, because replication faithfully copies the corruption.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger words: 'RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes across Regions' (Aurora Global Database), 'writes in multiple Regions' (DynamoDB global tables), 'protect against accidental deletion' (versioning/PITR/backup, NOT replication), 'the cheapest way to survive an AZ outage' (Multi-AZ). Discriminator: replication protects against infrastructure loss; backups protect against human and application error.

example.scenario: An engineer proposes enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication as the company's protection against a developer accidentally deleting production objects.
example.answer: Enable S3 Versioning (with MFA Delete or Object Lock as appropriate) rather than relying on replication.
example.why: Replication propagates the change, so a delete marker or overwrite is faithfully copied to the destination and the 'backup' is destroyed alongside the original. Versioning preserves prior object versions in place and Object Lock or MFA Delete prevents permanent removal, which is what protects against human error.

rows: Single AZ or data centre loss
Only if backups are copied cross-Region
Covered with Vault Lock / Object Lock / cross-account copy

gotchas: Replication is not backup: deletes and corruption replicate too.
Aurora Global Database secondary Regions are read-only until you fail over; a managed planned failover is different from an unplanned detach-and-promote.
DynamoDB global tables resolve conflicts last-writer-wins — the application must tolerate that.
Cross-Region replication of encrypted data requires a KMS key in the destination Region and permissions to use it.
S3 Cross-Region Replication only replicates objects created after replication is enabled; use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects.
Multi-Region designs still need per-Region quotas, AMIs, and IAM in place — this is exactly what ARC readiness checks audit.
numbers: Aurora Global Database: typically <1 s cross-Region lag, ~1 min RTO for managed planned failover
S3 Replication Time Control SLA: 15 minutes for 99.99% of objects

sections.title: Backup, restore, and DR patterns
sections.summary: Know what each backup mechanism covers, how long it is retained, and — the part that gets tested — what the restore actually produces.

concepts.name: AWS Backup: plans, vaults, Vault Lock, and cross-Region/cross-account copy
concepts.explain:
AWS Backup is the centralised, policy-driven backup service and it is the default 'least operational overhead' answer whenever the stem involves multiple services or multiple accounts. A backup plan contains rules; each rule sets a schedule (cron or frequency), a backup window with a start-window and completion-window, a lifecycle (transition to cold storage after N days, delete after N days — note cold storage requires a minimum 90-day retention, so the delete-after must be at least transition-to-cold plus 90), a target vault, and optionally a copy action to another vault in another Region or account. Resources are attached to the plan by resource assignment, and assigning by tag is the pattern the exam wants for 'automatically include new resources' — you tag the resource and it is picked up on the next run, with no plan edit.
Backup vaults hold recovery points and are encrypted with a KMS key. Vault Lock makes retention immutable: governance mode allows users with explicit permissions to remove the lock, while compliance mode is irreversible once the cooling-off period (a grace window of at least 3 days) elapses — nobody, including the root user and AWS, can delete recovery points before their retention expires. Compliance mode is the answer to WORM and ransomware-protection requirements.
Additional features tested: continuous backup enables point-in-time restore, to within one second and up to 35 days back, for the resources that support it — Amazon S3, RDS, Aurora, and SAP HANA on EC2 — rather than only discrete snapshots (DynamoDB point-in-time recovery is a native DynamoDB feature, not an AWS Backup continuous backup, and RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters are not supported); cross-account copy requires AWS Organizations and a destination vault policy; restore testing runs scheduled automated restores and reports whether they succeed and how long they take, which is how you prove RTO; and Backup Audit Manager evaluates controls (are all tagged resources backed up? is retention at least N days? is cross-Region copy configured?) and produces compliance reports.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger words: 'centrally manage backups across accounts and services', 'automatically include newly created resources' (tag-based assignment), 'backups must not be deletable even by an administrator' (Vault Lock compliance mode), 'prove that our restores work' (restore testing), 'report on backup compliance' (Backup Audit Manager). Discriminator: tag-based resource assignment for automatic inclusion; compliance mode for irreversible immutability.

example.scenario: A regulator requires that database backups cannot be deleted before seven years, by anyone, including account administrators and the root user.
example.answer: Store the recovery points in an AWS Backup vault with Vault Lock in compliance mode and a seven-year retention.
example.why: Compliance mode becomes immutable after the cooling-off period, so no principal — including root — can shorten retention or delete recovery points before they expire. Governance mode can be removed by a sufficiently privileged principal, and an SCP or bucket policy can be changed by whoever holds the permission to change it.

rows: Yes — by principals with explicit permission
Internal policy enforcement, room for correction
No — irreversible after the cooling-off period

gotchas: Tag-based resource assignment picks up new resources automatically; listing resources by ARN does not.

Cold storage transition requires a minimum 90-day retention, so retention must be at least transition days + 90 — which is also why continuous backups (35-day maximum) can never transition to cold storage.
Compliance-mode Vault Lock cannot be undone after the cooling-off period — test in governance mode first.
Cross-account copy requires AWS Organizations and a vault access policy on the destination; cross-Region copy needs a KMS key usable in the destination Region.
The backup start window is when the job may start, not when it must finish; jobs that do not start within the window are marked failed or expired.
AWS Backup can restore an EC2 instance from a backup of the instance (AMI plus volumes), but restoring a single EBS volume produces a new volume you must attach yourself.
numbers: Cold storage minimum retention 90 days
Vault Lock compliance cooling-off minimum 3 days

concepts.name: EBS snapshots, DLM, Fast Snapshot Restore, AMIs, and RDS backups vs snapshots vs PITR
concepts.explain:
EBS snapshots are incremental and stored in S3 in an AWS-managed account: only changed blocks are stored after the first snapshot, and deleting an intermediate snapshot never breaks later ones because AWS re-parents the blocks. Snapshots are Regional; copying a snapshot to another Region (or re-encrypting with a different KMS key) is a separate copy action. A restored volume is lazily loaded from S3, so the first read of each block is slow — Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) pre-provisions the volume so it delivers full performance immediately, at an hourly per-snapshot-per-AZ charge. Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates snapshot and AMI creation and retention by tag, and is the lightweight alternative to AWS Backup for EBS-only estates. An AMI is a snapshot set plus launch metadata; sharing an encrypted AMI across accounts requires sharing the customer managed KMS key too, because the default aws/ebs key cannot be shared.
RDS gives you three restore-shaped things and the exam loves to separate them. Automated backups run daily in the backup window plus continuous transaction logs, with a retention period of 0 to 35 days (0 disables backups) — they enable point-in-time recovery to any second within retention, typically to within about five minutes of the present. Automated backups are deleted when you delete the instance unless you take a final snapshot or use retained automated backups. Manual snapshots persist until you explicitly delete them, and can be copied cross-Region and shared. Cross-Region automated backup replication replicates the automated backups (and PITR capability) to a second Region.
The most-tested fact: restoring an RDS snapshot or performing a point-in-time restore always creates a NEW DB instance with a NEW endpoint. It never restores in place. So the runbook is: restore → verify → repoint the application (change the connection string, or better, use a CNAME you control or RDS Proxy) → adjust security groups and parameter groups, which do not always carry over as you expect. Aurora additionally offers Backtrack (MySQL-compatible), which rewinds the existing cluster in place to a point in time within the backtrack window, typically in minutes, with no new cluster and no endpoint change — the right answer when a bad migration script must be undone quickly.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger words: 'after the point-in-time restore the application still fails' (new endpoint), 'undo a bad update quickly without a new cluster' (Aurora Backtrack), 'restored volume performance is poor initially' (Fast Snapshot Restore), 'share an encrypted AMI with another account' (share the CMK too), 'automate daily EBS snapshots by tag' (DLM). Discriminator: RDS restore always produces a new instance; Backtrack is the only in-place rewind.

example.scenario: A bad deployment corrupted data in an RDS for MySQL database at 14:05. The team performed a point-in-time restore to 14:00, the restore completed successfully, but the application continues to serve corrupted data.
example.answer: Repoint the application to the restored instance's new endpoint (and update security groups and parameter group as needed).
example.why: A point-in-time restore always creates a new DB instance with a new endpoint DNS name; the original instance is untouched and still serving the corrupted data. Re-running the restore or extending the backup retention changes nothing because the restore itself already succeeded.

rows: Same cluster rewound in place, same endpoint
New table (restore to a new table name)
New resource of the same type

gotchas: RDS PITR and snapshot restores create a new instance with a new endpoint — always include the repointing step.
Deleting an RDS instance deletes its automated backups (unless retained); manual snapshots survive.
Backup retention of 0 disables automated backups and PITR entirely.
DynamoDB PITR restores to a NEW table; it cannot overwrite the existing table, and it does not restore auto scaling settings, IAM policies, or CloudWatch alarms.
EBS snapshot restores are lazily loaded — first-touch reads are slow unless Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled (which is charged per snapshot per AZ per hour).
Sharing an encrypted snapshot or AMI requires a customer managed KMS key shared with the target account; the default aws/ebs key cannot be shared.
Aurora Backtrack is MySQL-compatible only, must be enabled before you need it, and does not exist for Aurora PostgreSQL.

DynamoDB PITR 35 days
Aurora Backtrack window up to 72 hours
RDS PITR granularity ~5 minutes behind current time

concepts.name: S3 and FSx durability controls, and choosing a DR pattern by RPO/RTO
concepts.explain:
S3 protects data with layered controls. Versioning keeps every version and turns a delete into a delete marker — it is the baseline defence against accidental overwrite and deletion, and it cannot be disabled once enabled, only suspended. MFA Delete (configurable only by the bucket owner's root user, using the CLI) requires an MFA code to permanently delete a version or change versioning state. Object Lock provides WORM in governance mode (bypassable with a specific permission) or compliance mode (nobody, including root, can delete before the retention date), plus legal holds with no expiry; Object Lock requires versioning, can be turned on either at bucket creation or later on an existing versioned bucket, and once enabled cannot be turned off (nor can versioning then be suspended). Replication (same-Region SRR or cross-Region CRR) copies new objects asynchronously and requires versioning on both buckets; existing objects need S3 Batch Replication. S3 Replication Time Control adds a 15-minute replication SLA with metrics. FSx (Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS) takes automatic daily backups with a configurable retention plus user-initiated backups, and Windows/ONTAP/OpenZFS also expose file-level snapshots (shadow copies) for self-service restore.
DR patterns are ranked by RPO/RTO against cost, and the exam expects the ordering and the operational steps. Backup and restore: backups copied cross-Region, nothing running; RPO hours, RTO hours to a day; cheapest; failover means provisioning infrastructure from IaC then restoring data. Pilot light: data continuously replicated and core services (database, AMIs, IaC) present but application tier switched off; RPO minutes, RTO tens of minutes; failover means scaling up compute and switching DNS. Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully functional copy running all the time; RPO seconds to minutes, RTO minutes; failover means scaling out and switching DNS. Multi-site active/active: full capacity in both Regions serving live traffic; RPO near zero, RTO near zero; most expensive; 'failover' is removing one Region from the routing.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger words: 'RTO of 4 hours, lowest cost' (backup and restore or pilot light), 'RTO of minutes, must not run full capacity' (pilot light or warm standby), 'zero downtime, serve from both Regions' (active/active), 'objects must be immutable for compliance' (Object Lock compliance mode), 'a user permanently deleted an object' (versioning + MFA Delete). Discriminator: match the stated RTO/RPO number to the pattern, then pick the cheapest pattern that meets it.

example.scenario: A company needs an RTO of about 20 minutes and an RPO of about 5 minutes for a three-tier application in a second Region, while keeping standby costs low. Database data is already replicated cross-Region.
example.answer: Implement a pilot light: keep the replicated database and the AMIs/IaC in the second Region with the application tier stopped, and on failover launch the application tier and switch Route 53 to the secondary.
example.why: The replicated data satisfies the 5-minute RPO while leaving the compute tier switched off satisfies the cost constraint, and launching a pre-baked application tier from IaC fits inside a 20-minute RTO. Backup and restore cannot meet a 20-minute RTO because infrastructure and data must both be rebuilt, and warm standby or active/active pays for running capacity the requirement does not need.

columns: What runs in the DR Region
rows: Deploy IaC, restore data, repoint DNS
Remove the failed Region from routing

gotchas: Versioning cannot be turned off once enabled — only suspended, and existing versions remain.
MFA Delete can only be enabled by the bucket owner's root account using the CLI or API, not the console.
S3 replication requires versioning on both source and destination and only covers objects written after it is enabled — use S3 Batch Replication to backfill.

Object Lock compliance mode blocks deletion by every principal including root until the retention date passes — the only way out early is closing the AWS account; governance mode is bypassable with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention.
A DR plan that is never tested has an unknown RTO — AWS Backup restore testing and ARC readiness checks are the tested ways to prove it.
Pilot light and warm standby both still need per-Region service quotas, AMIs, and IAM roles pre-created, or the failover fails on the day.
Cross-Region copies of KMS-encrypted data need a KMS key in the destination Region and grants for the copying principal.

Requirement phrase mapping: 'least operational overhead' = managed service or tag-based automation; 'without changing the application' = DAX / RDS Proxy / Multi-AZ / CloudFront; 'cannot be deleted by anyone' = Vault Lock or Object Lock compliance mode; 'react within seconds' = Serverless v2, on-demand capacity, or a warm pool.

Eliminate by mechanism first: a Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads, Route 53 public health checkers cannot probe a private IP, ECS service auto scaling cannot add EC2 instances, and replication cannot protect against deletion.
numbers: S3 Replication Time Control SLA 15 minutes
FSx automatic daily backup retention configurable (commonly 0-90 days)
